papers.title: Sleep trajectories in pregnancy: associations with trauma exposure, PTSD, and postpartum depression.
papers.abstract: Sleep during the perinatal period is often highly disrupted due to maternal biopsychosocial changes that accompany pregnancy. Poor sleep quality is a symptom of PTSD, while insomnia often emerges after a traumatic event and commonly co-occurs with PTSD. Trauma exposure as well as insomnia have been linked to increased risk for postpartum depression (PPD). The current study examined sleep trajectories across pregnancy and into the postpartum period, the impact of trauma exposure and PTSD on these sleep trajectories, and associations between these sleep trajectories and PPD. Participants completed psychiatric diagnostic evaluations for PTSD and other mental health conditions, as well as validated self-ratings of insomnia and depressive symptoms at four time points across pregnancy and at 6 weeks postpartum. Participants were categorized into one of four groups: (a) trauma exposure with PTSD, (b) trauma exposure with another mental health condition, (c) trauma exposure with no mental health conditions, or (d) no reported trauma exposure or current mental health conditions. Longitudinal growth mixture modeling revealed two distinct sleep trajectories across pregnancy: poor sleep (28.5%) and normative sleep (71.5%). Trauma-exposed participants with PTSD or other mental health conditions were more likely to have poor sleep profiles. Participants with poor sleep profiles had significantly higher depressive symptoms. These findings support the need for targeted interventions addressing insomnia in trauma-exposed pregnant women with psychiatric sequelae to improve outcomes during and after pregnancy.

papers.title: Effects of nighttime graduated compression tights on overnight changes in lower-limb circumference in healthy young women with subjective leg swelling: A randomized crossover trial.
papers.abstract: BackgroundTransient lower-limb swelling may occur in healthy young women during daily life. This study examined whether wearing graduated compression tights during sleep enhanced overnight reductions in lower-limb circumference and affected subjective sleep quality or morning fatigue.MethodsIn this randomized, open-label, two-period crossover trial, female university students aged 18-28 years with subjective lower-limb swelling were assigned 1:1 to compression-first or no-compression-first sequences. Each 14-day period was separated by a 7-day washout. With compression, participants wore graduated compression tights during sleep after daytime acclimation. Co-primary outcomes were between-condition differences in overnight circumference change at the ankle, calf, and thigh. Secondary outcomes were subjective sleep quality and morning fatigue. Self-reported morning leg swelling was assessed at each time point. Mixed-effects models were used, with Holm adjustment for three primary outcomes.ResultsForty-six participants were randomized and 44 completed both periods. Compared with no compression, compression resulted in greater overnight reductions at the ankle (least squares mean difference, -0.23 cm; 95% confidence interval, -0.33 to -0.13; adjusted p = 0.0001), calf (-0.35 cm; -0.52 to -0.18; adjusted p = 0.0004), and thigh (-0.28 cm; -0.47 to -0.08; adjusted p = 0.0066). Perceived morning leg swelling was less likely with compression (30.6% vs. 58.4%). The OSA-MA sleep-length factor was lower at Time3 (nominal p = 0.03), but no other sleep-related outcome or morning fatigue differed significantly. No adverse events were reported.ConclusionsWearing graduated compression tights during sleep enhanced overnight reductions in lower-limb circumference. Although the differences were modest (approximately 2-4 mm) and their clinical importance remains uncertain, the accompanying reduction in perceived morning swelling suggests that these changes may have perceptible relevance to participants. Nighttime compression may facilitate the overnight reduction of transient lower-limb swelling under everyday living conditions.

papers.title: Developing a Theory-Based Sleep Hygiene Education Intervention for Adults with Insomnia: An Intervention Mapping and Content Validation Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep hygiene education (SHE) is commonly used in insomnia management, yet its observed effectiveness is modest, potentially reflecting limitations in its implementation, including simplified content, limited standardization, and suboptimal delivery formats. This study aimed to systematically develop a theory-based SHE program for adults with insomnia. The SHE intervention was developed following Phase I of the Medical Research Council framework and operationalized using Steps 1-4 of intervention mapping. Stakeholders, including 10 experts and 10 individuals with insomnia, were engaged throughout development to review and validate the program content, enhance its acceptability, and ensure its appropriateness. The resulting theory-based SHE program comprises two integrated components: (1) an educational module addressing insomnia knowledge, evidence-based sleep hygiene behaviors, and self-regulatory strategies for initiating and sustaining practice; and (2) brief follow-up telephone consultations designed to reinforce adherence and support implementation planning. Experts and individuals with insomnia endorsed the program's overall appropriateness, with minor refinements suggested for specific elements. This study presents a structured development and content validation of a theory-driven SHE program informed by behavioral science, empirical evidence, and stakeholder input. The intervention targets key limitations of traditional SHE approaches and provides a strong foundation for future feasibility testing.

papers.title: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor-Associated Bruxism: Neuropharmacologic Mechanisms and Clinical Implications.
papers.abstract: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)-associated bruxism is an increasingly recognized medication-associated phenomenon, although its incidence, neuropharmacologic mechanisms, and optimal management remain incompletely understood. This focused narrative review examines the clinical evidence, proposed mechanisms, and therapeutic implications of SSRI-associated bruxism. Available literature demonstrates recurring temporal associations between SSRI initiation or dose escalation and the emergence of jaw clenching, tooth grinding, pain, and related orofacial symptoms across multiple agents. Proposed mechanisms are multifactorial and may involve altered monoaminergic regulation within central motor networks, including serotonergic-dopaminergic interactions, 5-hydroxytryptamine (serotonin) receptor 1A (5-HT1A) signaling, and possible noradrenergic contributions; however, these mechanisms remain unconfirmed in affected patients. Adjunctive buspirone is the most consistently described pharmacologic strategy and may permit the continuation of an otherwise effective SSRI, although evidence for benefit remains primarily case-based. The literature is limited by heterogeneous bruxism definitions, inconsistent differentiation between awake and sleep manifestations, variable antidepressant exposures, and sparse objective physiologic assessment. Prospective studies using standardized assessment methods and controlled treatment designs are needed to clarify incidence, susceptibility, pathophysiology, and treatment response.

papers.title: The Use of Montelukast in Pediatric Asthma and Anti-Inflammatory Effects - Easy Choice or a Balancing Act?
papers.abstract: Montelukast is a selective cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1 antagonist with an established, though nuanced, role in the management of asthma and allergic rhinitis. By inhibiting leukotriene-mediated signaling, montelukast targets a pathway involved in bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, vascular permeability, eosinophil recruitment, cytokine release, and airway remodeling. Available evidence indicates that montelukast may reduce several markers of allergic inflammation, including fractional exhaled nitric oxide, peripheral and tissue eosinophilia, eosinophil-derived mediators, adhesion molecules, selected cytokines, and markers related to airway remodeling. These effects are most consistently demonstrated in asthma and allergic rhinitis, while evidence in chronic urticaria, atopic dermatitis, and other inflammatory conditions remains limited or exploratory. Montelukast's once-daily oral administration and age-adjusted pediatric formulations make it a practical option in selected children, particularly when inhaled therapy is difficult or adherence is problematic. However, montelukast should not be regarded as a direct substitute for corticosteroid-based anti-inflammatory therapy. Current evidence and guideline positioning support its use mainly as an add-on controller, or an alternative when more efficacious treatment is contraindicated. The benefit-risk balance is further shaped by concerns regarding neuropsychiatric adverse events, especially in children, although evidence remains heterogeneous. Current data show no increased risk of severe, diagnostically coded neuropsychiatric events, yet milder sleep-related and behavioral symptoms are consistently reported, so that caution and active monitoring remain warranted. Overall, montelukast remains a biologically plausible and clinically useful therapy, but its value depends on appropriate patient selection and realistic expectations of its anti-inflammatory potential.

papers.title: Neonatal Pain Assessment After Night Shifts in NICU Professionals: A Within-Subject Exploratory Eye-Tracking Study.
papers.abstract: Night-shift work may influence attention and emotion processing, potentially affecting clinical assessment. We investigated whether neonatal pain evaluation and associated visual-attentional and pupillary responses differed between rested and post-night-shift assessments in experienced NICU professionals. In this prospective within-subject study, 20 NICU professionals evaluated 42 standardized video clips of term neonates exposed to nonnoxious, short noxious, or prolonged noxious stimuli. Participants were assessed after at least 1 day off work and within 2 h after completing one or more consecutive night shifts. Pain ratings, eye-tracking metrics, and pupil diameter were compared between conditions. Overall pain ratings did not differ significantly between rested and post-night-shift assessments (3.56 ± 0.69 vs. 3.61 ± 0.72; p = 0.643; Cohen's d = 0.11). Pupillary responses also showed no statistically significant differences. Exploratory eye-tracking analyses suggested reduced visual exploration after night-shift exposure, including fewer visits across several areas of interest and shorter fixation duration on the infant's body. These secondary analyses were unadjusted for multiple comparisons and should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating. No statistically significant differences in neonatal pain ratings or pupillary responses were detected following routine night-shift work, whereas exploratory eye-tracking measures suggested differences in visual-attentional patterns. Given the small, selected sample and exploratory design, these findings do not establish equivalent or preserved performance between conditions. Larger prospective studies incorporating objective sleep measures and clinically relevant outcomes are warranted.

papers.title: Perioperative Anesthetic Considerations for Temporal Bone Tumor Resection in Fibroblast Growth Factor 23 (FGF23)-Related Tumor-Induced Osteomalacia: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors (PMTs) are uncommon, predominantly benign neoplasms frequently associated with dysregulated phosphate metabolism through the overproduction of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). Elevated levels of FGF23 lead to phosphate depletion, which may impair tissue oxygen delivery, central respiratory drive, and respiratory muscle function. Systemic manifestations may include osteomalacia and neuromuscular dysfunction, with an increased risk of respiratory and cardiovascular complications. PMTs often present with nonspecific clinical findings and may remain unrecognized during the perioperative period, presenting significant challenges for anesthetic planning and management. We report the case of a 72-year-old male with tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO), a right temporal mass, and multiple comorbidities, including hypertension and obstructive sleep apnea. The patient reported progressive headaches and general weakness. After neurosurgical evaluation, he underwent elective surgical excision under general anesthesia. Intraoperatively, he developed hypotension following induction of anesthesia, requiring vasopressor support with ephedrine boluses and a continuous phenylephrine infusion. The remainder of the procedure was uneventful, and the patient was extubated and transferred to the intensive care unit in stable condition. This case highlights the importance of recognizing potential complications in patients with metabolic abnormalities presenting with PMTs, particularly disturbances in phosphate homeostasis that may have significant anesthetic implications. The use of video laryngoscopy, judicious administration of neuromuscular blocking agents, and an individualized anesthetic strategy facilitated secure airway management, minimized cervical manipulation, and supported an uneventful recovery. Moreover, integrating anesthetic selection with comprehensive perioperative planning is essential to address the metabolic, musculoskeletal, respiratory, and hemodynamic challenges associated with TIO, particularly in patients with significant comorbidities.

papers.title: From Mechanistic Evidence to Clinical Translation: A Narrative Review of Chinese Herbal Medicine for Insomnia.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is one of the most common sleep disorders and a major public health problem worldwide. Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) is widely used as a complementary and alternative approach for chronic insomnia. Clinical studies have reported preliminary evidence of benefit for Chinese herbal formulas, whereas mechanistic research has examined single herbs, extracts, active constituents, and compound formulas using multi-omics analysis, network pharmacology, molecular prediction, and experimental validation. However, clinical studies are typically small and of inconsistent methodological quality, with limited long-term follow-up, while mechanistic evidence remains fragmented and lacks systematic integration and translational validation. These limitations restrict the development of CHM interventions from experimental evidence to clinically testable interventions for insomnia. This narrative review evaluates existing research across five translational dimensions, namely chemical characterization and preparation quality, exposure and pharmacodynamic evidence, mechanism and target validation, sleep-related clinical endpoints, and safety. It aims to clarify the current state of research on CHM interventions for insomnia and to identify key limitations and priorities for future research. Most available evidence comes from preclinical studies, which suggest that CHM may influence sleep-related processes through γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and serotonergic signaling, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis-autophagy balance, and the brain-gut-microbiota axis. Much of this evidence reflects changes in biochemical markers or pathway activity, while only a few studies directly test target function. Clinical studies provide preliminary evidence of short-term improvements in subjective sleep outcomes. However, clinical translation remains limited by insufficient evidence for objective sleep improvement and long-term efficacy and safety. Future work should carry a few well-characterized interventions through the full evidence chain, prioritizing standardized preparations, exposure and pharmacodynamic assessment, objective sleep endpoints, long-term follow-up, and safety.

papers.title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing and Sleep Fragmentation in Relation to Atrial Fibrillation Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is one of the most prevalent cardiac arrhythmias worldwide. This study aimed to evaluate the association between sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), primarily assessed using the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), and AF risk, with additional analysis of sleep fragmentation parameters such as wake after sleep onset (WASO) and arousal index (AI). This systematic review and meta-analysis followed Cochrane Handbook recommendations and PRISMA guidelines, with protocol registration in PROSPERO (No. 127490). Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational cohort studies assessing sleep disturbances and AF were included. MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, and Scopus were searched from inception to February 2026. Extracted data included study characteristics, demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, and sleep metrics. Outcomes were incident and recurrent AF. A random-effects model was applied. Twenty-one cohort studies (611,898 participants) were included. SDB was associated with increased incident AF risk (RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.41-1.97; I 2 = 66.5%), with consistent Bayesian estimates. A dose-response relationship showed a 2% increase in AF risk per unit rise in AHI. For AF recurrence, 11 studies (n = 1810) demonstrated a significant association (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.40-1.72; I 2 = 0%), supported by Bayesian analysis. Sleep disturbances are significantly associated with both incident and recurrent AF and may represent modifiable risk factors.

papers.title: Step-by-Step Protocol for Fluorescence-Based Analysis of Uptake in Transporter-Expressing Xenopus laevis Oocytes.
papers.abstract: Xenopus laevis oocytes are widely used as a heterologous expression system for investigating the function of membrane proteins due to robust expression of heterologous protein and a low endogenous transport background. Traditionally, transporter activity in oocytes has been assessed using electrophysiology or radiolabeled uptake assays, approaches that are constrained by the requirement for electrogenicity of the transport process, availability of radiolabeled compounds, and instrumentation. Here, we describe a fluorescence-based uptake assay that enables direct and rapid quantification of transporter activity using a fluorescence plate reader. The protocol uses the Arabidopsis thaliana sucrose transporter 1 (SUC1) and its fluorescent substrate esculin as a case for how to set up the assay. The workflow includes optimizing assay conditions, sample preparation, fluorescent measurements, and downstream data analysis using R. This method can readily be adapted to other transporter-substrate pairs, and it supports applications such as transporter inhibitor screening, mutational analysis, characterization of kinetic properties, or indirect substrate specificity testing through competition assays. Overall, this protocol provides a simple and scalable alternative to traditional techniques, eliminating the need for radiolabeled compounds or electrophysiology while enabling easy quantitative assessment of transporter activity. Key features • Provides a simple, plate reader-based fluorescence uptake assay for quantifying transporter activity in Xenopus laevis oocytes. • Adaptable to any transporter with a compatible fluorescent substrate, supporting rapid testing of substrate specificity indirectly through competition assays or mutant screening. • Includes a complete workflow from assay setup and conduction to data analysis, suitable for both initial characterization and routine functional testing of membrane transporters.

papers.title: Association of Burning Mouth Symptoms with Sleep Quality, Stress and Xerostomia in Middle-Aged and Elderly Patients - a Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Burning mouth syndrome (BMS) is a long term syndrome of oral pains that is prevalent among the middle aged and the aged people. It is usually associated with poorly understood symptoms, including sleeping difficulties, psychological stress and xerostomia (dry mouth). The objective of the systematic review was to establish the association between the burning mouth symptoms and sleep quality, stress and xerostomia, through a systematic review of the literature at hand. A thorough electronic database search was carried out leading to the identification of 10 eligible studies, according to a set of inclusion and exclusion criteria. The results showed that BMS is closely linked with low sleep quality, high levels of psychological distress and perceived dry mouth, which may lead to a multifactorial interaction, which determines the extent of symptoms and the quality of life of patients. This research paper is added to the scientific literature as it summarizes existing evidence and emphasizes the need to thoroughly assess and treat patients with BMS using multidisciplinary approaches.

papers.title: Intermittent hypoxia interventions for inducing ventilatory acclimatization to high altitude?
papers.abstract: Accumulation of ∼200 h of hypoxia exposure (pre-acclimatization) has been suggested to prevent the development of acute mountain sickness when a person is subsequently exposed to high altitude. These pre-exposures are typically undertaken intermittently at or near the place of residence, primarily during sleep in hypoxic tents, and are likely to induce effective ventilatory acclimatization. However, the physiological consequences of different modes of intermittent hypoxia (IH) exposure on ventilatory acclimatization remain largely obscure and are the subject of much controversy. The aim of this review is therefore to summarize and discuss the findings of relevant studies and draw on our long-term practical experience to address the effects of IH exposure on ventilatory acclimatization and to provide suggestions for effective pre-acclimatization. We provide a balanced overview of studies investigating the effects of different types of altitude/hypoxia exposure on the hypoxic ventilatory response and renal compensation to hyperventilation-induced respiratory alkalosis. Although it has been demonstrated convincingly that the hypoxic ventilatory response can increase by 50%-100% with only a few short IH sessions (1 h per day for 7 days), the available data on the effects of IH on renal compensation do not permit definitive conclusions to be drawn. Long-term exposure to IH over several weeks appears to induce renal compensation effectively, allowing for a full ventilatory response and favourable oxygenation at high altitude. To clarify definitively which strategies are most suitable, long-term systematic investigations of various IH strategies are urgently needed.

papers.title: Post-dexamethasone cortisol levels in non-functioning adrenal incidentalomas: a pooled individual participant data analysis.
papers.abstract: Non-functioning adrenal incidentalomas (NFAI) are defined by 1 mg-dexamethasone suppression test (F-1mgDST) cortisol levels < 1.8 µg/dL. However, many individuals with NFAI may exhibit subtle hypercortisolism associated with increased cardiometabolic and skeletal risk. The aims of the present study are to compare F-1mgDST distributions between individuals with NFAI and population-based controls and to explore whether alternative F-1mgDST thresholds would meaningfully modify patient classification. This is a pooled individual participant data analysis of 7 studies evaluating cortisol secretion in patients with type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis and/or fragility fractures, hypertension, or adrenal incidentalomas. The study included 1681 participants (915 NFAI, 766 controls) with F-1mgDST < 1.8 µg/dL. Data included age, sex, body mass index (BMI), F-1mgDST, and adrenocorticotroph hormone (ACTH). We assessed the between-group differences in F-1mgDST and ACTH and the accuracy of different F-1mgDST thresholds for identifying NFAI. Compared to controls, patients with NFAI had lower age and ACTH levels (62.1 ± 9.8 and 59.8 ± 12.0 years, 25.1 ± 14.1 pg/mL and 16.3 ± 10.4, respectively, p < 0.001 for all comparisons), but higher BMI and F-1mgDST values (28.1 ± 4.9 and 29.0 ± 5.0 kg/m2, 1.04 ± 0.37 µg/dL and 1.13 ± 0.39 µg/dL, respectively, p < 0.001 for all comparisons) and were more less frequently females (48.0% and 38.6%, respectively, p < 0.001). A propensity score analysis performed on 730 patients and 730 age-, BMI- and gender-matched controls confirmed these findings. We did not identify any F-1mgDST threshold with an accuracy exceeding 60% for distinguishing controls from patients with NFAI. The F-1mgDST threshold the best balance between sensitivity (54.8%) and specificity (57.2%) was set at 1.1 µg/dL (30 nmol/L), although with a low accuracy of 55.8%. Individuals with NFAI have higher F-1mgDST levels than controls. More than 40% overlap exists in F-1mgDST values between NFAI and controls.

papers.title: Effect of web-based education on NIV-related side effects and insomnia severity in COPD patients using home NIV: a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the effect of web-based education on NIV-related side effects and insomnia severity in COPD patients using home noninvasive ventilation (NIV). This randomized controlled trial was conducted with 75 patients between October 2023 and May 2024. Data were collected using the S³-NIV Questionnaire and the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI). The intervention group received web-based education regarding NIV-related side effects and insomnia management. Independent samples t-tests were used to compare numerical descriptive characteristics between groups, while Pearson chi-square and Fisher's exact tests were used for categorical variables. Repeated-measures ANOVA was performed to evaluate changes over time and between groups. Compared with the control group, the intervention group demonstrated significantly higher total S³-NIV Questionnaire scores and higher respiration, sleep, and side-effect subscale scores at weeks 4 and 8. Significant group × time interaction effects were observed for total S³-NIV scores (p < 0.001, η²p = 0.753) and ISI scores (p < 0.001, η²p = 0.352). For insomnia severity, no significant between-group difference in ISI scores was observed at Week 4, whereas ISI scores were significantly lower in the intervention group at Week 8. Web-based education may help improve patient-reported NIV-related symptoms and reduce insomnia severity in patients with COPD using home NIV. These findings suggest that web-based educational interventions may support symptom management and patient adaptation in clinical practice.

papers.title: EORTC QLQ-C30 symptom components and their functional correlates during adjuvant chemotherapy for early breast cancer: a multivariate analysis. Data from GEICAM/2003-02 study.
papers.abstract: Understanding how multiple symptoms jointly impact functioning is essential for interpreting patient-reported outcomes (PROs) in oncology. We aimed to characterize the main dimensions underlying change-from-baseline (CFB) in symptom scores during adjuvant chemotherapy for early breast cancer, and to examine their associations with functional outcomes. We analyzed EORTC QLQ-C30 CFB scores from 820 patients enrolled in the GEICAM/2003-02 trial. Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to summarize correlated symptom changes into a smaller number of components, and graphical LASSO network modelling was applied to explore relationships among Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) domains. Associations between components and functional scales and global health status were assessed using Spearman correlations. Three components were identified in the pooled sample, explaining 53.6% of the variance: a dominant general symptom burden component, a gastrointestinal component, and a diarrhea-specific component. The general component, primarily defined by fatigue, pain, appetite loss, insomnia, nausea/vomiting and dyspnea, showed consistent negative correlations with all functional scales and global health status. Similar patterns were observed across treatment arms, although gastrointestinal-related components differed. Graphical LASSO identified fatigue as the symptom most strongly connected to functional impairment. Symptom changes during chemotherapy are not independent, but follow a multivariate structured pattern in which a general symptom burden, anchored by fatigue, plays a central role in functional decline. These findings suggest that multivariate approaches may provide a complementary exploratory framework for summarizing correlated patterns of treatment-related burden and generating hypotheses regarding PROs. Trial registration number ClinTrials.gov: GEICAM/2003-02: NCT00129389.
papers.journal: Quality of life research : an international journal of quality of life aspects of treatment, care and rehabilitation

papers.title: EEG Microstates are Not Associated with Psychotic Symptoms, Neurocognitive Domains or Psychosocial Functioning in Adolescents and Young Adults with Clinical High Risk for Psychosis.
papers.abstract: EEG microstates are brief and discrete topographic patterns of electrical brain activity. Microstates last for 60-120 milliseconds, are thought to represent transient, quasi-stable neural networks, and traditionally four distinct classes (A-D) are distinguished. One of the core concepts of present neuroscience is that neuroimaging is able to capture meaningful networks of brain activity, which can be translated into specific cognitive functions. Following this idea, each microstate might correspond to specific core brain functions. Importantly, these cognitive functions are impaired in mental disorders. Clinical high-risk (CHR) refers to a state associated with an increased risk of developing psychosis. Previous research has demonstrated consistent microstate alterations in CHR individuals (especially in class D), as well as in psychosis. However, the neurobiological and functional meaning of microstate alterations in CHR populations is still elusive. Since the CHR state is associated with reduced neurocognition (e.g., processing speed, verbal memory, executive functions) in combination with specific clinical symptoms and impairments in psychosocial functioning, relationships between resting-state microstates and these domains were examined in a large cross-sectional cohort of CHR individuals (n = 100). Contrary to our expectations, no significant correlations were found for these clinical measures. The finding suggests that while microstate parameters may differ between CHR individuals and controls, these alterations do not seem to directly reflect the neurobiology of clinical symptoms or neurocognitive and psychosocial functions. EEG microstate deviations as candidate trait biomarker therefore require further investigation and validation in longitudinal studies to establish their stability and predictive value.

papers.title: Neuromonitoring of perioperative microembolization and its association with postoperative stroke after carotid endarterectomy.
papers.abstract: This study aims to assess whether perioperative microembolization can identify patients at risk for postoperative stroke. A total of 257 carotid endarterectomy procedures in 254 patients were analyzed (154 symptomatic, 103 asymptomatic). Neuromonitoring, combining transcranial Doppler ultrasonography and continuous electroencephalography, was utilized to evaluate cerebral perfusion and detect microembolic signals (MES). Monitoring covered the entire intraoperative phase and a standardized 20-minute postoperative observation window. Postoperative stroke occurred in seven patients, six of whom were symptomatic prior to the procedure. In exploratory penalized regression analyses, higher postoperative MES counts (OR 1.02 per MES, 95% CI 1.01-1.04; p < 0.001) and an intraoperative burden of ≥ 10 MES (OR 6.06, 95% CI 1.40-34.78; p = 0.016) were associated with postoperative stroke. Symptomatic patients exhibited a significantly higher embolic burden (6.7 ± 13.3 vs. 2.2 ± 5.0, p = 0.004). Beyond its role in guiding selective shunting, transcranial Doppler monitors the occurrence of microembolization, which could serve as a potential indicator of perioperative stroke. In this exploratory analysis, both an intraoperative burden of 10 or more MES and sustained postoperative microembolization were associated with postoperative stroke. Given the low number of events, these findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation before they can guide perioperative management.

papers.title: Neurophysiological Correlates of Target-Related Visual Attention Processes as a Function of Reward in Connection with Schizotypy.
papers.abstract: In everyday life, we constantly select and perceive relevant information while suppressing irrelevant sensory input. This selection process is governed by the interaction between bottom-up and top-down attention mechanisms. Recent studies also highlighted the influence of reward on attention, with monetary rewards shown to enhance task performance and modulate stimulus salience. Schizotypy, conceptualized as a continuum ranging from healthy states to schizophrenia symptoms, provides a framework for the investigation of these mechanisms in non-clinical populations. This study investigated the behavioral and neurophysiological correlates of visual attention and reward processing, and their relationship with schizotypy traits. Thirty-six healthy participants were divided into two groups which performed a visual attention task with salient distractors and rewarded (target reward group, TR) or not rewarded (no reward group, NR) target stimuli while EEG was recorded. Additionally, schizotypy was assessed using the Schizotypal Personality Questionnaire (SPQ). The results showed that salient, but task-irrelevant distractors increased response times compared to target-only trials irrespective of reward. On the neurophysiological level, distractors decreased target prioritization in the NR group. Furthermore, participants with higher scores on the negative schizotypy dimension showed stronger target prioritization, especially in the absence of salient distractors. These findings suggest that monetary rewards can modulate attentional control mechanisms and that negative schizotypy traits are linked to altered attentional prioritization.

papers.title: Effects of anti-inflammatory dietary education on sleep disturbances among patients with breast cancer undergoing chemotherapy: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: This randomized controlled trial evaluated the effects of anti-inflammatory dietary education on sleep disturbances and inflammatory biomarkers in patients with breast cancer undergoing chemotherapy. A total of 132 patients with sleep disturbances were randomized to receive either a 12-week anti-inflammatory dietary education program based on the energy-adjusted dietary inflammatory index (E-DII) or usual care. Sleep disturbances were assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) at baseline and at 12 weeks. Additional outcomes included inflammatory biomarkers, E-DII scores, and quality of life (QoL). Treatment effects on continuous outcomes were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) under the intention-to-treat principle. The proportions of participants with sleep disturbance (PSQI ≥ 8) at 12 weeks were compared between groups using a completer analysis. Of the 132 participants, 116 (87.9%) completed the 12-week assessment. In the completer analysis, the proportion of participants with sleep disturbance at 12 weeks was significantly lower in the intervention group than in the control group (49.2% vs. 78.9%, P < 0.001). The intervention group demonstrated greater reductions in PSQI (β = - 2.10; 95% CI: - 3.01, - 1.18; P < 0.001) and E-DII scores (β = - 1.23; 95% CI: - 1.98, - 0.47; P = 0.002) and improved overall QoL (β = 14.07; 95% CI: 8.61, 19.52; P < 0.001). Furthermore, levels of interleukin-1β, interleukin-6, and C-reactive protein were significantly reduced, whereas interleukin-10 increased (all P < 0.05). Anti-inflammatory dietary education reduced sleep disturbances and improved QoL in patients with breast cancer undergoing chemotherapy and was accompanied by favorable changes in inflammatory biomarkers. ChiCTR2500097053. Registered on 11 February 2025.
papers.journal: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer

papers.title: Disrupted daily rhythms in light exposure and wrist temperature are associated with metabolic risk markers and obesity.
papers.abstract: Light exposure is the primary external synchronizer of the body's internal clocks and daily rhythms. This study investigated whether light exposure and wrist temperature real-life 24-h rhythms are associated with obesity and metabolic risk markers in a large cohort of healthy adults. A total of 809 individuals from the ONTIME-MT study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03036592) were included. Mean age was 37.47 ± 14.24 years, mean BMI was 25.75 kg/m², and 71% were women. Daily light exposure and wrist temperature were continuously monitored over seven consecutive days under free-living conditions. Principal component analysis was used to identify factors capturing circadian-related functioning. Cross-sectional study. Healthy adults of European descent from a Spanish cohort assessed in an ambulatory setting. Obesity-related and metabolic risk parameters. Three factors emerged in both the light exposure and wrist temperature rhythm domains, explaining approximately 73% and 80% of the total variance. In both domains, Factor 1 accounted for the largest proportion of variance (≈41-42%) and reflected overall rhythm robustness, characterized by higher relative amplitude and greater interdaily stability, together with average light exposure or wrist temperature levels. Higher light exposure Factor 1 was associated with lower serum triglyceride concentrations (P = 0.013). Wrist temperature Factor 1 was associated with lower BMI and body fat percentage in women, as well as lower insulin, HOMA-IR and triglyceride levels, and higher HDL-cholesterol (all P < 0.05). Mediation analyses showed that interdaily stability of wrist temperature rhythms may affect the association between light exposure stability and triglyceride levels, accounting for approximately 11% of the total effect (P = 0.021). In this large real-life cohort, less robust daily rhythms of light exposure and wrist temperature were consistently associated with adverse metabolic profiles. These findings highlight the potential of circadian-related markers derived from wearable technologies as non-invasive indicators of metabolic risk. ONTIME-MT study; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03036592.

papers.title: Smartphones, digital media use, and sleep in young adolescents.
papers.abstract: The purpose of this study was to examine the association between smartphone ownership and usage behaviors and sleep duration and quality among adolescents aged 11 to 13 years, and whether these associations differed by sex. We analyzed data from 1510 participants in the 2024 Life in Media Survey (LIMS), an online cross-sectional survey of 11- to 13-year-olds in Florida. Logistic regression models adjusted for appropriate confounders assessed associations between smartphone ownership and 6 usage behaviors, including device location at night; in-bed usage; evening usage time; online posting; notifications; and exposure cyberbullying, and the outcomes of sleep duration and trouble sleeping. Sex-stratified analyses were conducted to assess for effect modification. Smartphone ownership was associated with lower odds of insufficient sleep and trouble sleeping; however, several usage behaviors were strongly linked to poorer sleep. Keeping a smartphone in hand/in bed, using it in bed, posting publicly online, spending more than 2 hours on the device in the evening, and experiencing cyberbullying were each associated with increased odds of insufficient sleep duration and trouble sleeping. Using the phone in bed showed the strongest associations (aORs up to 13 for trouble sleeping). Cyberbullying consistently predicted all adverse sleep outcomes. Sex-stratified results showed variation in some associations. In early adolescence, how smartphones are used, rather than merely owning one, has substantial implications for sleep. Behaviors such as nighttime proximity, in-bed use, late‑evening screen time, and exposure to online stressors were most detrimental. Promoting healthier bedtime practices and reducing negative online experiences may improve sleep in this age group.

papers.title: Divergent associations of weekly and seasonal sleep variability with 1-year glycemic change in Chinese adults.
papers.abstract: Sleep variability is often examined as a unitary construct, yet its metabolic relevance may differ by temporal scale. Although social jetlag, reflecting weekly misalignment between sleep and social schedules, is associated with worse glycemic control, the longitudinal relationship of naturally occurring seasonal sleep variability with glucose metabolism remains unclear. We aimed to evaluate and contrast the associations of annualized social jetlag and seasonal sleep variability with 1-year changes in fasting blood glucose. We analyzed data from 357 Chinese adults in a longitudinal design. Sleep was recorded via diary over three consecutive days in each season, enabling computation of annualized social jetlag and intra-individual standard deviations of sleep duration and timing across seasons. Fasting blood glucose was measured at baseline and 1 year later. Compared with minimal social jetlag (<0.25 hour), high social jetlag (≥0.5 hour) was associated with a 6.1% increase in fasting glucose (95% CI: 1.3, 11.2). In contrast, greater seasonal variability in sleep duration (per 1-hour increase in standard deviations) was associated with a 6.5% decrease in glucose (95% CI: -11.1, -1.7). An interaction was observed for MTNR1B rs1387153 (Pinteraction = .04), with an inverse association between seasonal variability in wake-up timing and glucose present in C-allele carriers but absent in TT homozygotes. Weekly social jetlag and seasonal sleep variability show opposing longitudinal associations with glycemic change. Maintaining a natural degree of seasonal sleep plasticity is associated with better glucose regulation, and this relationship appears to be modified by genetic variations in MTNR1B.

papers.title: Self-reported sleep health is more than a combination of multiple objective sleep measures.
papers.abstract: The self-reported Ru-SATED questionnaire is a psychometrically validated measure of multidimensional sleep health. Ru-SATED is increasingly examined in relation to health outcomes; however, its relationship to behavioral sleep is unknown. This study describes the combinations of bed-measured sleep health features that are associated with the Ru-SATED sleep health score. Sleep Number bed users (N = 2674, Mage = 52.4 ± 16.2, 55.2% women) completed the Ru-SATED 4.0 multidimensional sleep health scale and contributed past-month smart bed data (7-28 days). Associations between Ru-SATED and bed features (duration, efficiency, regularity, timing) were modeled using: (1) Spearman correlations; (2) multivariable regression with bed features included additively; (3) polynomial regression with complex interactions among bed features combined with novel graphical techniques; and (4) non-parametric tree-structured regression. Individual bed measures had weak correlations with Ru-SATED (r = 0.04-0.21; R2-adjusted = 0.002-0.040). Models incorporating multiple bed features explained larger proportions of variance in Ru-SATED (Additive regression R2-adjusted = 0.078; polynomial regression R2-adjusted = 0.084; tree-structured regression R2-adjusted = 0.090). Across models, bed-measured duration (ΔR2 = 0.015-0.018), regularity (ΔR2 = 0.011-0.019), and efficiency (ΔR2 = 0.010-0.015) made the largest contributions to Ru-SATED, followed by timing (ΔR2 = 0.001-0.003). Individuals with the best Ru-SATED score had good bed-measured regularity, efficiency, duration, and timing, while those with the worst Ru-SATED had some combination of poor regularity, duration, efficiency, and/or timing. Ru-SATED was associated with combinations of behavioral bed measures, above any single bed measure. Bed-measured duration, regularity, and efficiency made the strongest contributions. Findings further validate the multidimensional sleep health framework and may assist with presenting clinically relevant information regarding patient sleep health patterns and goals.

papers.title: Association of obstructive sleep apnea with pancreatic cancer in high-risk patients under surveillance in CAPS and PCYST cohorts.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) has been linked with increased cancer incidence and mortality. We hypothesized that OSA may be a risk factor for neoplastic progression among patients undergoing pancreatic cancer surveillance. Retrospective medical record review of two Johns Hopkins Hospital cohorts undergoing pancreas surveillance; patients with familial/genetic risk enrolled in the Cancer of the Pancreas Screening (CAPS) study and patients with incidentally detected pancreatic cysts, enrolled in the PCYST study. Time-to-progression to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and neoplastic progression (either PDAC, high-grade dysplasia or pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor) were compared by OSA status, adjusting for covariates. OSA was diagnosed prior to or during surveillance in 174 (19.5%) of 893 patients in CAPS and 376 (23.7%) of 1585 patients in the PCYST cohort. In the combined cohorts, OSA was associated with increased risk of progression to PDAC (unadjusted HR: 3.12, 95% CI: [1.82, 5.34], p < 0.001). OSA was also associated with male sex, higher BMI, fatty liver, fatty pancreas, diabetes, and history of smoking (all p < 0.01). After covariate adjustment, OSA remained associated with PDAC risk (adjusted HR: 2.56 [1.44, 4.55], p = 0.001). Factors associated with neoplastic progression included OSA (adjusted HR: 1.93 [1.25, 2.97], p = 0.003), increasing age (age-per 5-years adjusted HR: 1.14 [1.05, 1.24], p = 0.003), fatty liver (adjusted HR: 1.76 [1.19, 2.60], p = 0.005), and diabetes (adjusted HR: 1.77 [1.16, 2.71], p = 0.008). Patients undergoing pancreatic surveillance for their familial/genetic risk and/or incidentally detected pancreatic cysts have a greater likelihood of developing pancreatic cancer if they've been diagnosed with OSA.
papers.journal: Pancreatology : official journal of the International Association of Pancreatology (IAP) ... [et al.]

papers.title: Ganoderma lucidum polysaccharides alleviate cognitive impairment in sleep-deprived mice: Association with gut microbiota remodeling.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) can impair cognitive function through multiple processes, including systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, and synaptic dysfunction, yet effective interventions remain limited. Therefore, this study investigated whether Ganoderma lucidum polysaccharides (GLP) could alleviate SD-induced cognitive impairment and whether such effects were accompanied by changes in gut microbiota, fecal metabolism, and indicators related to the microbiota-gut-brain (MGB) axis. In a chronic SD mouse model, GLP administration not only improved memory performance and anxiety-like behaviors but also increased hippocampal BDNF levels and the expression of the synapse proteins PSD-95 and SYP. Integrated 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics revealed that GLP remodeled the gut microbial landscape, enriching genera such as Kurthia and Roseburia, suppressing Escherichia-Shigella, and shifting fecal metabolic profiles, with elevated gamma-glutamylglycine and reduced cyclic melatonin as representative metabolic signatures. These peripheral changes were accompanied by reduced serum lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and inflammatory cytokines, alongside a more favorable hippocampal profile characterized by enhanced Nrf2-related antioxidant responses, improved AQP4 distribution, and diminished Aβ1-42 deposition. Correlation analyses further linked taxa responsive to GLP, particularly Kurthia and Escherichia-Shigella, to metabolite shifts, behavioral outcomes, and hippocampal markers. Collectively, these findings indicate that the cognitive benefits of GLP in SD mice are closely associated with coordinated changes across the MGB axis, providing a foundation for further exploration of GLP as a functional food candidate.

papers.title: NOD1 contributes to reduced postoperative memory performance induced by preoperative sleep deprivation and anesthesia/surgery in mice.
papers.abstract: Nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing protein 1 (NOD1) recognizes bacterial peptidoglycan fragments and regulates inflammatory responses. However, its role in perioperative memory performance remains unclear. This study investigated the involvement of NOD1 in the hippocampal CA1 region and gut-related alterations in postoperative memory performance. Mice underwent preoperative acute sleep deprivation, anesthesia/surgery, or both. Behavioral testing, hippocampal transcriptomics, fecal metagenomic sequencing, western blotting and immunofluorescence were performed. Iba1 promoter-driven NOD1 knockdown in the hippocampal CA1 region and Lyz1-/- mice were used to investigate the involvement of NOD1 in the hippocampal CA1 region and intestinal lysozyme, respectively. No statistically significant synergistic or facilitating interaction between sleep deprivation and anesthesia/surgery was detected. Significant main effects were observed in the object location memory test (OLMT) and novel object recognition test (NORT), whereas the Y-maze showed only a post hoc difference between the SD + Sur and Con groups. The reduced postoperative memory performance was accompanied by increased NOD1 expression, an elevated p-p65/p65 ratio and Iba1-related changes in the hippocampal CA1 region, together with gut microbiota dysbiosis and increased ileal expression of lysozyme. Both Iba1 promoter-driven NOD1 knockdown and Lyz1 deficiency reduced NOD1 expression, p65 phosphorylation and Iba1-related changes. Iba1 promoter-driven NOD1 knockdown improved memory performance, whereas Lyz1 deficiency improved OLMT and Y-maze performance and showed a trend toward improved NORT performance. Hippocampal CA1 NOD1, gut microbiota dysbiosis and ileal lysozyme may contribute to reduced postoperative memory performance associated with preoperative acute sleep deprivation and anesthesia/surgery.

papers.title: Transcranial magneto-acoustic stimulation modulates M1-PPN spike-LFP coupling and improves motor dysfunction in parkinsonian rats.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate whether transcranial magneto-acoustic stimulation (TMAS) improves motor dysfunction in Parkinson's disease (PD) model rats and whether its effects are associated with modulation of bidirectional spike-local field potential (LFP) coupling between the primary motor cortex (M1) and the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN). Two primary cohorts (n = 24 each) comprised WT + Sham, PD + Sham, and PD + TMAS groups (n = 8/group). An independent supplementary healthy-control experiment included newly allocated WT + Sham and WT + TMAS groups (n = 8/group; 16 rats total), both of which followed the Experiment 1 workflow. Pre-treatment APO rotation counts were compared between the two PD groups as a functional index of lesion severity. Motor performance, TH and c-Fos immunofluorescence, and in vivo M1-PPN electrophysiology were evaluated. Spike-LFP coherence and phase-locking value (PLV) were compared among the three primary groups separately within each putative neuronal class, behavioral state, and frequency band. APO rotation counts did not differ between PD + Sham and PD + TMAS rats before treatment in either experiment. TMAS-treated PD rats showed improved behavioral performance, and the pattern of differences in M1-PPN spike-LFP coherence and PLV relative to PD + Sham rats varied across frequency bands, behavioral states, and putative neuronal classes. At the terminal histological assessment, PD + TMAS rats showed a higher proportion of TH-positive cells in the SNc than PD + Sham rats. In the independent healthy-control experiment, WT + TMAS did not significantly differ from WT + Sham in most behavioral indices or TH-positive cell proportion, but it showed a shorter pole-test turning time and a higher c-Fos-positive cell proportion. TMAS ameliorated motor deficits in PD model rats and was associated with frequency band, behavioral-state, and putative-class-dependent changes in M1-PPN spike-LFP coupling. These findings provide preliminary evidence supporting TMAS as a potential noninvasive neuromodulation strategy for PD-related motor dysfunction, while the disease specificity of the electrophysiological effects remains to be established.

papers.title: Synchronized audiovisual stimulation enhances neural entrainment: convergent evidence from complementary EEG biomarkers.
papers.abstract: Rhythmic sensory stimulation modulates oscillations via frequency-specific entrainment, but synchronized auditory contributions remain unclear, and periodic-aperiodic decomposition has not been applied to audiovisual entrainment. Forty adults received visual stimulation at 8, 20, and 40 Hz, alone (VF) or synchronized with binaural beats of identical frequencies (VF + BB). EEG was analyzed using power spectral density (PSD), topographical mapping, Sample Entropy (SampEn), Lempel-Ziv Complexity (LZC), Phase-Locking Regularity (PLR), and IRASA to separate periodic (SSVEP) from aperiodic (1/f) contributions. Visual flicker induced frequency-specific entrainment, and binaural beats modulated responses frequency-dependently. At 8 Hz, flicker elicited a periodic SSVEP; adding binaural beats enhanced this component and increased aperiodic activity. At 20 Hz, synchronized audiovisual stimulation enhanced both periodic and aperiodic components. At 40 Hz, IRASA showed no significant periodic modulation; VF + BB produced a widespread increase in aperiodic offset and exponent, absent under VF alone. VF + BB reduced SampEn across all frequencies and increased PLR at 8 and 20 Hz, whereas LZC decreased at 8 Hz and increased at 20 Hz. Synchronized audiovisual stimulation produced frequency-dependent changes in EEG spectral organization. At 8 and 20 Hz, adding binaural beats enhanced the periodic SSVEP component, with changes in the aperiodic background. At 40 Hz, conventional PSD showed increased gamma activity, but periodic-aperiodic decomposition did not reveal significant periodic enhancement; audiovisual stimulation primarily altered aperiodic offset and exponent. Complementary regularity and phase-based measures showed frequency-dependent temporal changes. Findings highlight combining conventional spectral analysis, periodic-aperiodic decomposition, and complementary EEG biomarkers to characterize synchronized audiovisual stimulation.

papers.title: Methodology for identification of depleted metallic uranium and natural metallic uranium by portable gamma spectrometer.
papers.abstract: The requirement to distinguish between depleted metallic uranium (DU) and natural metallic uranium (NU) is essential in nuclear forensics, regulatory enforcement, nuclear fuel fabrication and environmental monitoring. Traditional laboratory-based methods offer high accuracy but are impractical for on-site measurement. This research develops a portable gamma spectrometry-based methodology for identifying DU and NU in real-time, non-destructively. The study utilizes a NaI(Tl) based gamma spectrometer to measure characteristic emissions from uranium isotopes and its daughter products. Key gamma peaks, particularly those at 92 keV (234Th) and 186 keV (235U), were analysed to derive isotopic ratios indicative of the material type. Emphasis was given on choosing right gamma peak and adjustment for x-ray contribution in 92 keV peak. Estimated activity ratio of 235U to 234Th of five natural uranium samples was greater than or equal to 0.046 and the activity ratio of five depleted uranium sample found to be less than 0.046, which validated the methodology. The results demonstrate that, with proper calibration, and spectral analysis, portable gamma spectrometry can serve as an effective tool for real-time uranium isotope identification in applications ranging from nuclear safeguards and non-proliferation to environmental monitoring and emergency response.
papers.journal: Applied radiation and isotopes : including data, instrumentation and methods for use in agriculture, industry and medicine

papers.title: Radiosurgical capsulotomy for treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder through a network neuroscience lens.
papers.abstract: Severe, treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) remains disabling despite optimized pharmacotherapy and exposure and response prevention (ERP). Radiosurgical capsulotomy is an irreversible ablative intervention reserved for highly selected patients. This narrative review examines evidence from structural MRI, diffusion imaging, functional connectivity, electrophysiology, and radiobiology. The search was supplemented by a reproducible PubMed search across eight prespecified modules (856 records before and 739 after deduplication), with an audited 102-record core SRS/OCD set. Structural lesion mapping and a small longitudinal diffusion study support investigating pathway involvement alongside lesion volume, but do not establish a validated network mechanism or individualized targeting biomarker. Functional MRI and EEG findings in OCD and connectivity studies of other interventions provide complementary evidence but require cautious cross-modality extrapolation. Single-session irradiation must be distinguished from thermal capsulotomy; dose, prescription isodose, irradiated volume, and delayed toxicity require joint interpretation. We use "functional disconnection" as a hypothesis concerning downstream effects of tissue injury, not evidence of a nonablative or reversible treatment. Priorities include harmonized longitudinal imaging, dose-volume-connectivity analyses, cognitive and behavioral surveillance, and controlled evaluation of ERP timing. Current evidence supports a network-informed research framework without establishing a post-radiosurgery plasticity window or superiority of connectivity over conventional planning variables.

papers.title: Longitudinal associations between screen time activities and working memory neural signatures in adolescents: Sex differences and contextual moderation.
papers.abstract: Adolescent screen media activity (SMA) has increased, yet its longitudinal associations with neurocognitive development and mental health remain unclear across activities and contexts. This longitudinal cohort study used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (release 6.0) with four assessments (baseline, year 2, year 4, and year 6). Participants were recruited across 21 U.S. sites to reflect demographic diversity. Children with valid neuroimaging and behavioral data were included, adjusting for demographic, behavioral, and psychiatric confounders. Working memory (WM) neural signature (NS) scores were derived using elastic net classification of EN-back fMRI activation during 0-back and 2-back conditions. SMA included time spent video gaming, watching television, texting, and social media. Cognitive performance was measured using EN-back accuracy, and mental health symptoms using Child Behavior Checklist internalizing and externalizing scores. Moderation analyses examined family conflict, sleep disturbance, and physical activity. The analytic sample included 9931 participants (47.2% female). Higher NS scores were associated with better 0-back and 2-back accuracy. Greater video gaming, texting, and television watching were associated with lower NS scores. Sex-stratified analyses showed among males, more screen time was associated with lower NS scores, a multivariate measure of how separable neural activation patterns are between the 2-back and 0-back conditions. These associations were specific to the EN-back task and were adjusted for general cognitive ability. Higher degrees of family conflict increased the association between NS with texting, and video gaming and externalizing symptoms among males. Sleep disturbance and physical activity also moderated associations with internalizing and externalizing symptoms, with sex-specific patterns. WM-related neural function was associated with cognitive performance and SMA engagement, differing by sex and environmental context, highlighting complex associations between neurocognitive development, media use, and mental health.

papers.title: Combined Prenatal Environmental Stressors Induce Suprachiasmatic Degeneration with Unexpected Behavioural Resilience in Long-Evans Rats.
papers.abstract: Environmental heat stress and displacement adversity during pregnancy pose significant risks to neurodevelopment, particularly in regions with high maternal mortality and population displacement. The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), the brain's master circadian pacemaker, is vulnerable to prenatal environmental insults, yet the combined impact of thermal and psychosocial stressors on SCN development remains unexplored. We examined the effects of prenatal heat stress and displacement-like conditions on SCN morphology and behaviour across two critical developmental stages. Twenty-five timed-pregnant Long-Evans rats were exposed to heat stress (38-40°C, 2h daily), displacement conditions (overnight food/water restriction plus overcrowding), combined stressors, or control conditions from gestational days 15-20. Male offspring were assessed at postnatal days 10 (neonatal) and 30 (juvenile). Heat exposure induced significant maternal hyperthermia (2.5-2.9°C elevation). Histological analysis revealed marked SCN cellular degeneration across stress groups at both developmental stages, characterised by reduced cell counts, pyknotic nuclei, and disrupted tissue architecture. Despite structural damage, juvenile behavioural testing revealed paradoxical outcomes: combined stress exposure reduced anxiety-like behaviour in the elevated plus maze, enhanced sociability in three-chamber testing, while preserving recognition memory. Growth analysis demonstrated preferential brain sparing despite reduced somatic growth, with significantly elevated brain-to-body weight ratios in stress-exposed animals. These findings demonstrate that prenatal environmental stressors cause lasting SCN damage but trigger adaptive behavioural responses. The dissociation between structural vulnerability and functional adaptation suggests complex neurodevelopmental programming with implications for populations experiencing heat exposure and displacement adversity.

papers.title: Night-time sling use improves sleep, pain, and anxiety early after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair: a retrospective study.
papers.abstract: Postoperative sleep disturbance is common after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair (ARCR). Although abduction braces are routinely used to protect the repair, they may impair sleep and comfort. This study evaluated whether replacing the brace with a simple sling at night was associated with improved early postoperative outcomes. This retrospective comparative study included 92 patients undergoing ARCR. Patients were classified according to routine postoperative immobilization: continuous abduction-brace use (brace group, n = 46) or daytime brace use with a simple sling during habitual overnight sleep (sling group, n = 46). Sleep quality was assessed using a visual analog scale (VAS) and the Medical Outcomes Study Sleep Scale (MOS-SS), pain using a numerical rating scale (NRS), anxiety using the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA), and shoulder function using the Constant-Murley Score (CMS). Patient satisfaction was also evaluated. The sling group had better sleep VAS scores at postoperative night 3, week 1, and week 6 (all p < .001). At week 6, the sling group had longer sleep duration (7.02 vs. 6.61 hours, p = .023), lower MOS-SS 10-item composite scores (31.98 vs. 35.20, p < .001), lower pain NRS scores (1.46 vs. 2.22, p < .001), and lower HAMA scores (4.89 vs. 6.20, p < .001). CMS values were comparable between groups throughout follow-up, while satisfaction was higher in the sling group (100% vs. 78.26%, p < .001). Nighttime sling use after ARCR was associated with better early sleep, less pain and anxiety, and greater satisfaction without an observed difference in functional recovery. Because treatment allocation was nonrandom and structural healing was not assessed, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.

papers.title: An adaptive, variable-length test for certifying electroencephalographic spike-detection skill: A retrospective feasibility study.
papers.abstract: Determining whether an individual reader has sufficient electroencephalographic (EEG) spike-detection skill is challenging due to limited expert agreement. We evaluated whether modeling skill in interpretable signal-detection terms-discrimination ability separate from response tendency-could power an adaptive, variable-length test that can reliably and efficiently assess reader competence. We analyzed a multirater dataset containing 20 521 EEG segments and 2574 rater sessions. Case signal was estimated from multirater labels, and each reader was modeled using signal-detection parameters: discrimination skill σ and response bias t . Among 368 calibration-eligible raters across five skill tiers, we used a stratified 50/50 train-validation split to select a certification threshold σ ⋆ in training and to apply it in validation. We replayed an adaptive test on each rater's historical responses, using sequential stopping to issue pass, fail, or retest decisions. The training-derived threshold was σ ⋆ = .815 (95% bootstrap confidence interval = .663 - 1.018 , Youden J = .828 ). In validation, pass rates preserved the expected tier ordering: experts 100% ( 14 / 14 ), experienced 100% ( 4 / 4 ), novices 14% ( 1 / 7 ), residents 0% ( 0 / 11 ), and crowd raters 7% ( 11 / 150 ). In the 81-rater adaptive replay, clear failures stopped near 20 trials, and passing experts required a median of 95 trials. Split-half replay showed intraclass correlation coefficient 3 , 1 = .87 for σ ̂ at stopping; there were no hard pass-fail reversals among raters whose two halves both reached decisive verdicts. A signal-detection framework quantified spike-identification skill in EEG readers, and adaptive testing estimated this skill reliably with fewer than 100 short EEG segments. This approach could provide a practical, scalable method for assessing EEG reading competence.

papers.title: Factors associated with premenstrual syndrome and menstrual pain in women of childbearing age.
papers.abstract: BackgroundThis study investigated variables associated with Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) and Menstrual Pain in women of childbearing age to provide foundational data for improving quality of life.ObjectivesThis study aimed to examine variables associated with premenstrual syndrome and menstrual pain among women of childbearing age.DesignA cross-sectional descriptive survey design was used.MethodsA survey of 245 women of childbearing age in the metropolitan area was conducted using online questionnaires. The data were analyzed with independent t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and multiple regression to identify factors associated with premenstrual syndrome and menstrual pain.ResultsIn the bivariate analyses, sleep quality, perceived daily stress, menstrual flow, analgesic use frequency, timing of severe menstrual pain, family history of perimenstrual discomfort, depression (CES-D), and perceived stress (PSS) were significantly associated with both PMS and menstrual pain (p < 0.05). In the multiple regression analyses, PMS was associated with VAS (B = 5.180, 95% CI: 3.33 to 7.03), CES-D (B = 1.395, 95% CI: 0.97 to 1.82), family history of perimenstrual discomfort (B = 9.987, 95% CI: 1.12 to 18.86), and timing of severe menstrual pain on Day 1 (B = -15.153, 95% CI: -24.43 to -5.88) or Day 2 (B = -12.210, 95% CI: -23.96 to -0.46). Menstrual pain was associated with MDQ (B = 0.014, 95% CI: 0.008 to 0.02), family history of perimenstrual discomfort (B = 0.996, 95% CI: 0.51 to 1.48), age (B = -0.057, 95% CI: -0.10 to -0.02), perceived daily stress, analgesic use frequency, and coping method for menstrual pain (p < 0.05).ConclusionIn this study, psychological and menstrual-related variables, including depression, perceived stress, family history of perimenstrual discomfort, PMS, and menstrual pain intensity, were associated with menstrual symptoms among women of childbearing age. These findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal relationships.

papers.title: Taking a clinical history in adolescents and adults presenting with seizures or epilepsy.
papers.abstract: Despite advances in EEG, neuroimaging, and other diagnostic technologies, a carefully obtained clinical history remains the cornerstone of diagnosis, classification, and treatment planning. However, structured guidance on history-taking that integrates state-of-the-art evidence and the updated 2025 International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) seizure classification is limited. We performed a review of evidence published between January 2000 and April 2026, supplemented by landmark earlier studies, ILAE position papers, and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines. Evidence was synthesized to develop a practical framework for obtaining and interpreting the clinical history in adolescents and adults presenting with a first seizure, recurrent seizures, or established epilepsy. We present a structured approach that follows the sequence of a clinical consultation, encompassing the presenting complaint, detailed event reconstruction, semiology, collateral witness accounts, smartphone video recordings, seizure triggers and temporal patterns, past medical history, medication review, family history, social factors, and safety issues. We discuss the diagnostic value of individual history elements, practical strategies for distinguishing epileptic seizures from functional/dissociative seizures and syncope, and the contribution of history-taking to seizure classification under the updated 2025 ILAE framework. We also summarize clinically relevant risk factors, comorbidities, and management implications that influence diagnostic accuracy and individualized care. Practical diagnostic questionnaires are provided to facilitate differential diagnosis and seizure classification, particularly for clinicians without specialist epilepsy expertise. A systematic clinical history, obtained from the individual and eyewitnesses and complemented by video recordings when available, remains the single most important diagnostic tool in epilepsy. Structured history-taking improves diagnostic accuracy, reduces misdiagnosis, supports accurate seizure classification, guides appropriate investigations, and provides the foundation for personalized management. This practical framework offers an evidence-based approach that can be readily incorporated into routine clinical practice and education across diverse healthcare settings.
papers.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape

papers.title: Inhaled β-myrcene alleviates insomnia in mice by modulating 5-HT1A/PKA signaling and the gut microbiota.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a major public health issue that impairs daily functions and quality of life. Sleep-onset difficulty, a common complaint among patients, is accompanied by reduced central serotonin (5-HT) function. β-myrcene from lavender has sedative-hypnotic effects via serotonergic pathways, but most previous studies used intraperitoneal injection, which causes stress and limits clinical translation. Here, we asked whether non-invasive inhalation of β-myrcene produced similar effects in a mouse model of insomnia with low 5-HT function, and explored the underlying mechanisms. β-myrcene was given to PCPA-induced insomnia mice by inhalation (with intraperitoneal injection as a pharmacodynamic control). In the inhalation group, sleep and behavior were evaluated using the amobarbital sodium sleep test and spontaneous locomotor activity test. ELISA, RT-qPCR, Western blot, and 16S rRNA sequencing were applied to study mechanisms. Inhaled β-myrcene shortened sleep latency and prolonged sleep duration. It also reduced oxidative stress and modulated GABA, 5-HT, and glutamate levels. These changes were accompanied by upregulation of mRNAs such as GABAARγ2 and 5-HT1A, as well as proteins including GAD65/67 and PKA, suggesting involvement of 5-HT1A/PKA signaling. Additionally, inhalation of β-myrcene was correlated with alterations in gut microbiota composition in PCPA-induced insomnia mice. Our findings indicate that inhaled β-myrcene is associated with sedative-hypnotic effects and alterations in gut microbiota composition in PCPA-induced insomnia mice, potentially involving modulation of 5-HT1A/PKA signaling.

papers.title: Single-Channel Electrophysiology Using a Miniaturized Montal-Mueller Planar Lipid Bilayer System for Recording a Synthetic K2P Channel.
papers.abstract: The functional reconstitution of ion channels into planar lipid bilayers provides a strategy to investigate channel activity at the single-molecule level. However, conventional Montal-Mueller bilayer systems typically require bulky experimental setups, manual chamber assembly, and relatively large recording volumes, which increase reagent consumption and may introduce additional sources of electrical noise due to extended wiring and external headstages. Here, we present a miniaturized, ready-to-use bilayer platform (BLMchipMM) integrated with a compact amplifier that enables stable single-channel recordings with reduced reagent consumption and simplified operation. This protocol describes the use of this system for performing single-channel electrophysiology measurements. Using this system, we reconstituted a synthetic K2P channel (ancTREK1) and used it as a proof-of-principle test protein to validate reconstitution and single-channel recording. Single-channel recordings show a current-voltage relationship in Mg2+-free symmetric K+ solutions, with conductance values consistent with those reported for TREK1 channels. The successful reconstitution of this K2P-like channel demonstrates the utility of this system for single-channel analysis in artificial membranes.

papers.title: Disability, Fatigue and Mental Health in Acute Versus Chronic Spinal Pain in the Gaza Strip: A Comparative Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Spinal pain is a major contributor to disability, but evidence comparing multidomain outcomes across acute and chronic stages remains limited in conflict-affected settings. This study aimed to compare disability, fatigue, psychological distress and sleep disturbance among patients with acute and chronic neck pain and low back pain (LBP) in the Gaza Strip. This comparative cross-sectional study included 410 adults attending outpatient physiotherapy at Nasser Medical Complex: acute neck pain (n = 101), chronic neck pain (n = 103), acute LBP (n = 102) and chronic LBP (n = 104). A 12-week cut-off defined acute and chronic pain. Disability was assessed using the Neck Disability Index (NDI)/Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) scores, fatigue using the Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS), psychological distress using the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4) and sleep disturbance using the PROMIS Sleep Disturbance Short Form 8a. Between-group comparisons, adjusted linear regression, correlation analyses, clinical-threshold analyses and logistic regression were performed. Chronic neck pain and chronic LBP were associated with higher disability, fatigue and psychological distress than acute pain (all primary comparisons p < 0.001). Sleep disturbance did not significantly differ between the acute and chronic groups. Adjusted analyses showed that chronic pain status remained associated with higher disability, fatigue and psychological distress. Fatigue was independently associated with chronic pain status in both neck pain and LBP models. Female participants reported higher psychological distress in both pain-location groups. Chronic spinal pain was associated with greater disability, fatigue and psychological distress but not with higher sleep disturbance. Findings support early multidimensional assessment, including screening for fatigue and psychological distress.

papers.title: Noise or clearance? Reframing plasma amyloid-β variability in Alzheimer's disease as a measurable clearance signal.
papers.abstract: Plasma biomarkers, and the amyloid-β 42/40 ratio in particular, are increasingly used to stage Alzheimer's disease and to stratify and monitor clinical trials, on the tacit assumption that a single measurement reflects a stable, steady-state level of pathology. A recent micro-longitudinal study that sampled plasma weekly for five weeks in people with Alzheimer's disease challenged that assumption, reporting that most participants varied by more than half in the amyloid-β 42/40 ratio over that short window. The reflexive response is to treat such movement as measurement noise to be averaged away. Here I argue that a meaningful part of it is unlikely to be noise. In healthy adults the same ratio is among the most stable plasma analytes, so instability concentrated in disease is difficult to attribute to the assay alone. Brain-to-blood clearance of amyloid-β is itself dynamic over days, rising with sleep and falling with fragmentation, apnoea, poor cerebral perfusion, autonomic dysregulation, and sedating or anticholinergic drugs. An instantaneous plasma value therefore partly reports the clearance state of the preceding night. This clearance account is kept distinct from analytical and pre-analytical variance, and from oligomeric amyloid-β dynamics, which are considered separately. The practical problem is not the variance itself but that we measure the molecule without measuring the physiological state that moves it. I propose that an inexpensive, repeatable, bedside index of that state, illustrated here with the Systemic BenBrik Geriatric Score, could be recorded alongside each plasma draw and modelled as a covariate, converting nuisance variance into interpretable signal. The prediction is falsifiable, and a validation design is outlined. This is a hypothesis, not a validated result; the illustrative index used here, the Systemic BenBrik Geriatric Score, is not a validated measure.

papers.title: Efficacy and Safety of Saffron and Ashwagandha for Stress-Related Mental Health Outcomes: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials.
papers.abstract: Saffron (Crocus sativus L.) and ashwagandha (Withania somnifera Dunal) are medicinal plants with emerging clinical evidence supporting their use for stress-related mental health conditions.
